With parliament not sitting and many people on holiday, there is less proper news than normal, which means the nonsense stories get (even) more attention than usual. We are almost slap bang in the middle of the month, and today we’ve got a silly season classic in Clacton, where Nigel Farage, the Reform UK candidate, is fighting a byelection in which his main opponent is a joke candidate who dresses up as a dustbin. Farage is not inherently silly. https://www.theguardian.com/culture/2026.text: ‘I think people are getting a bit tired of the Irish’ … Dara Ó Briain. Photograph: Pål Hansen/The Guardian View image in fullscreen ‘I think people are getting a bit tired of the Irish’ … Dara Ó Briain. Photograph: Pål Hansen/The Guardian Dara O Briain Interview ‘I remember going: oh hello!’ Dara Ó Briain on comedy, coolness, cruelty and finding his parents Sam Wollaston The standup has been the host of the panel show Mock the Week for more than two decades. As it returns to UK screens, he discusses its years as a macho bear pit, the dearth of jokes about Brexit – and why it’s important to punch up Wed 26 Aug 2026 05.00 EDT Last modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 05.50 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google D ara Ó Briain is still having photos taken when I arrive at the studio in west London. A comedian requires comedy pictures, so Pål, the photographer, has him sitting on the floor holding up a scroll of the rust-coloured paper that he’s using as a backdrop. It looks as if the roof is falling in on Ó Briain. He calls over to me. “We can tailor the interview to match the pictures,” he says. “Starting with: do you ever feel like you’re trapped in a box?” Shoot over, he ditches his jacket and we walk up the road to find a quiet corner in a pub. There’s a new season of Mock the Week, the topical satirical panel show that ran for 17 years on BBC Two until 2022 and has now been reborn on the free-to-air channel TLC. A roster of comedians make up two teams and compete in a faux gameshow, ostensibly to answer questions about the previous week’s news, but really just to be funny. Ó Briain, 54, has hosted it since the start. In the first iteration, regular guests included Hugh Dennis, Frankie Boyle and Ed Byrne, but up-and-coming comics were often included too. “It became a kind of debutante’s ball for people who’ve gotten to the top at Edinburgh and are ready to go on screen,” Ó Briain explains, not without pride. When Mock the Week was on the BBC, there were accusations that the mockery was directed to the right from the left. Ó Briain, who describes himself as “centre left”, says that had a lot to do with what was going on in Westminster: “For the vast majority of that time, there was a Tory government – Conservative PM after Conservative PM – so obviously we were looking at them.” But he also admits there was probably something to those accusations. “I don’t think anyone put an argument in favour of Brexit during the whole thing; nobody on Mock the Week was going: ‘Well, maybe sovereignty or whatever …’” The show featured the right-leaning comedians Geoff Norcott and Simon Evans, but the right isn’t as well represented in British comedy. Ó Briain isn’t sure why – perhaps because “the direction in which you punch matters or people don’t warm to it”, he says. “I have seen comics do jokes about, say, nurses always asking for money, and the audience go: ‘No, I don’t think that, we’re not coming with you on that one.’” Don’t mock the weak. But equally, he suggests, audiences don’t like it if you’re too far the other way – “too happy-clappy”. View image in fullscreen ‘It was generally seven men around the table: they were trying to find themselves, there were elbows’ … hosting Mock the Week. Photograph: BBC The other accusation aimed at Mock the Week was that it was vicious, mean and male – a bear pit of a show on which macho comedians elbowed each other out of the way in order to get their jibe in. Jo Brand didn’t like it when she went on. Again, Ó Briain says the criticism was fair. “It was generally seven men around the table: they were trying to find themselves; there were elbows.” But he points out that the programme started more than two decades ago, when this was the culture of shows of this kind (see also Never Mind the Buzzcocks). Ó Briain says he wouldn’t have liked to be a contestant. “I would have found it too staccato; I like to build up a head of steam on a piece of bullshit. But now it has become a lot more conversational.” While there’s plenty to converse about in the average week, some topics are riper for mockery than others. Trump, for example, isn’t the gift you might assume he is. “Particularly Trump 2, darker Trump. There’s not even the funny mistakes going on. Now, it’s self-parody, so utterly ridiculous that maybe it’s normalised the ridiculousness, to a certain extent. And you know, the joke’s already there – what are we adding to it? It would be like doing jokes about the Simpsons.” What about Keir Starmer? “Awful. He did nothing and said very little.” He means as a topic of discussion, rather than as a politician, although he wasn’t impressed with the way he ran the country, either. He’s not sure about Andy Burnham yet – they are still to mock one of his weeks – but he is amused by the process by which he came to power. “ Makerfield gets to pick the prime minister now , is that how it happens?” So what or who is a gift to Mock the Week? Peter Murrell and the SNP expenses scandal, he says: “Not quite a victimless crime, because I guess the people who made donations to the SNP were victims. But the details were so perfect: the number of video consoles, the £2,000 salt shaker [Murrell spent £2,618.16 on Lalique Feuilles pepper and salt grinders], the fact Nicola Sturgeon bent over backwards to act like she didn’t know her in-laws suddenly had a 30ft camper van .” They got some good mileage from that in the last season – more mileage than the camper van, which drove only from the showroom to the in-laws’ drive . Now, freed from the shackles of public service impartiality and scrutiny, and with more women involved, including Sara Pascoe , Maisie Adam , Laura Lexx and Angela Barnes , perhaps Mock the Week is a nicer place, even if it has many fewer viewers (a little more than 1 million when repeats are included) than the 3-million-plus it averaged in its BBC peak. Ó Briain wasn’t meant to be a comedian. He studied mathematics and theoretical physics at University College Dublin in the early 90s. He says he was a shy and self-conscious teenager, but pushed himself to join the debating society at UCD. During one debate, he told a joke: “It got a laugh, and a round of applause, and I remember this whoosh of adrenaline and me going: oh hello!” He still feels that whoosh, although the high isn’t so high and it might take a two-hour show, rather than one joke, to get there. But he loves the work and it takes him to cool places such as Athens, Barcelona and Stockholm (as well as Chatham, Dorking and Leicester). His two most recent tours have been less about the gags, more about the storytelling – and more personal. View image in fullscreen ‘The direction in which you punch matters’ … playing Latitude festival in Suffolk, 2017. Photograph: Rob Ball/Redferns Born in Bray, County Wicklow, Ó Briain was adopted into what he has described as “a stable home” and had a happy childhood. A few years ago, he decided to find out about his biological parents. “The plan wasn’t that it should be a show, it was just this thing I should investigate, because of normal human emotions. I always knew there was this story waiting to be found out, and then the impetus was that none of us are getting younger. I know of people who have found parents and then met them in a nursing home and they’ve had Alzheimer’s.” He realised the story wasn’t only about him after seeing the film Philomena . “I came out of the cinema with a sudden appreciation that this is actually not my story at all, I’m only a baby in it, but there’s a woman who got pregnant and went on this journey,” he says. “It’s her story and I should probably at the very least make contact in order to close that circle for her and let her know it was great and I found a lovely family and all that stuff.” It was hard – bureaucratically, emotionally – but he found her and they met up. It was awkward and strange. He got a bunch of new siblings. He told the story in his show So … Where Were We?, which won best tour at the Chortle awards in 2023. His next show, Re:Creation, which he’s been touring across Europe, tells the story of trying to track down his biological father. No spoilers (there are some dates left, plus it’s on Amazon Prime ), but it contains less sadness and anger than the previous set. “It’s a bit of a romp, with a twist towards the end that is delightful to deliver. Not quite The Sixth Sense, but kind of a gasp moment.” The problem now is what to do next. “Both stories just kind of emerge in a very tellable form. There’s no way of doing a third, no trilogy. Even as I’m doing it, enjoying telling the story, my head is going: ‘Yeah, next time, you’re going to actually have to do some work, write some jokes, because you’re not going to be gifted another parent to find, there isn’t another great family reveal,’” he says. Well, there is one possibility, surely. Maybe not a parent … He laughs. “Yes, the perfect thing would be a knock on the door and there’s a 25-year-old going: ‘I think …’ And I would go: ‘Thank you so much!’ Because this would be the only way you could extend the trilogy – if I was the father of a child given up for adoption.” It’s not going to happen, though. “I’ve done the audit, run it backwards in my head going: was there any situation that could have …?” He adds quickly: “I mean, I’ve had my checkered history. But I feel it’s all accounted for.” H is TV career started as a children’s presenter on the Irish state broadcaster RTÉ, while he was doing his first standup gigs on the Irish comedy circuit. He came to prominence hosting the topical panel show Don’t Feed the Gondolas from 1997 to 2001. His big break on the other side of the Irish Sea came in 2003, when he hosted The Live Floor Show on BBC Two, which led to appearances on Have I Got News for You. Since making his debut as Mock the Week’s host in 2005, Ó Briain has presented just about everything on television. Alongside the panel shows and the comedy, his interest in maths and physics continued. He has presented Stargazing Live from Jodrell Bank observatory with Prof Brian Cox; his hobby is astrophotography, which he does from his garden in London (“you can filter out all the light”); and he’s had many pops at bad science (hello, Gillian McKeith!) in his comedy. Even when chatting, he’ll borrow analogies from science. He says X, formerly known as Twitter, has become a black hole: “It’s got sucked into this thing and created so much density that it’s actually going to collapse under its own gravity.” (He has abandoned the platform.) The popularity of panel shows? They have their moments. “It’s like this graph of an extinction event: it goes back down again, but it never fully eliminates a small number of hard‑shelled animals who survive each time – the cockroaches who are the comedians at the bottom, never fully eliminated because they’re cheap and people like them, so they’ll come back.” View image in fullscreen ‘I know of people who have found parents and then met them in a nursing home and they’ve had Alzheimer’s.’ Photograph: Pål Hansen/The Guardian His own career, meanwhile, is more of a sine wave: “It goes up and down, but carries on.” Or is it a damped oscillation? “If you don’t pay attention, it gets smaller and smaller, asymptotically, until there’s only a tiny little vibration right at the very end and I’m sitting in an olive grove in Spain going: ‘ Buenos dias. ’” You’ll know, if you’ve seen him on stage or on TV, that Ó Briain’s delivery is superfast. Well, it doesn’t slow down over a quiet orange juice and lemonade. When he sets off on something, he’s like a rocket in space. I fire little thrusters (chip in with the odd question) in an attempt to steer the ship, but when something has that much momentum sometimes you just have to run with it. We go to many other places – solar eclipses , the World Cup, what to do if there’s a medical emergency in the audience, Arsenal’s transfer window , Blankety Blank, whether or not it’s cool to be Irish in London, but there isn’t space here … oh, go on then, just that last one. The answer is yes, but again it’s sinusoidal. “We are currently cool, but I think people are getting a bit tired of it, so probably it’s time for someone else to be cool for a while.” Whether he’s cool or not, 90 minutes with Dara Ó Briain is eye-opening, exhausting and delightful. He’s still talking when he gets into the car that has come to fetch him. It’s something about Melania Trump, although I’m not sure if it’s the documentary or the woman. And then it’s too late when I realise: I forgot to ask if he ever feels as if he’s trapped in a box. Mock the Week returns to TLC in the UK on 13 September at 9pm. https://www.omanobserver.om/article/1194.text: Oman Governorates Health Transport Rop Education His Majesty Environment Tourism Labour Community Weather Business Economy Markets Banking Energy Aviation Cars Property Tourism Features Lifestyle Arts Culture Food Travel Fashion Photography Films/tv Books Music The opera Weekend Sports Football Tennis Cricket Motor sports Athletics Golf NBA Other sports World Region Americas Europe Asia Africa Australia Scitech Science Technology DANUBE EXPOSES CLIMATE RISK TO NUCLEAR POWER Krisztina Than Published: 8:40 PM, Aug 14, 2026 SHARE Record low river levels have left Hungary straining to keep its nuclear power plant running ​while Romania was forced to shut down its last working reactor, ​raising questions about how to adapt atomic energy to an increasingly extreme climate. Reliance on river water for cooling nuclear reactors has long been an issue and has repeatedly led to reduced power output in the summer months, especially in France, which is more dependent on nuclear power than any other country. But the extremity of drought and heat this year in Europe, which has experienced more warming than any other continent, has added urgency to a debate about adaptation. Hungary was forced to cut its 2-gigawatt Paks nuclear plant's output to just over 10 per cent earlier this month, barely escaping a full shutdown for the first time in 44 years. It is now operating at 25 per cent of its capacity. Romania's ⁠state-owned Nuclearelectrica shut down its last working reactor on Thursday after efforts to divert cooling water to the plant were not enough. Nuclear power plants have the advantage of generating baseload power without carbon emissions, meaning they have a role in avoiding fossil fuel burning and tackling climate change. Romania and Hungary are both committed to expanding their nuclear production as a source of ample, domestic power, but that means finding a way to cool reactors that depends less on river water levels. Diana Ürge-Vorsatz, a professor at the Central European University in Vienna, said scientific modelling showed the ‌trend was for Central eastern Europe to become drier. "This is not only due to less rains, ​but because the soil moisture and in the groundwater ⁠levels have dropped over the past years and less precipitation and more heatwaves exacerbate soil drying", she said. At a conference last year of the ​Hungarian Hydrological Society, water engineers already warned that "flow patterns may become more ‌extreme and volatile" on the Danube, one of Europe's longest rivers. Now governments are seeking solutions under pressure as the emergency output cuts at Hungary's and Romania's nuclear plants have forced them to ask companies and households to cut power consumption. Among the measures proposed, Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar said on ​Wednesday his government would build what he referred to as a riverbed sill — a submerged, dam-like structure — to raise water levels. Also, two barges could be sunk on Friday to lift water levels to try to avert a shutdown, as the river is expected to shrink further in the coming days. The country is also reviewing the designs for the planned Paks 2 nuclear expansion that rely on the Danube for cooling. The former government of Viktor Orban selected Russia's Rosatom for the work without a tender in 2014. Romania's Nuclearelectrica operates two 706-megawatt reactors that account for a ‌fifth of the country's power production. They use Canadian CANDU technology that relies on heavy water, in which the hydrogen in water is replaced with a heavier isotope, to slow neutrons. The four ​reactors of Hungary's Paks plant, which generate around half of Hungary's power, are Russian-made pressurised water reactors. Both technologies pump water from the Danube for cooling and then release the water back ​into the river. By contrast, ‌Czech ⁠and Slovak nuclear power plants use wet cooling towers, which need less water, with the steam evaporated in the process emitted to the atmosphere. https://www.spokesman.com/stories/2026/a.text: Musician Kid Rock appears alongside President Donald Trump in the Oval Office. (Jabin Botsford/The Washington Post) Add Spokesman-Review on Google By Dan Lamothe and Noah Robertson Washington Post Days before the Army’s top officer was abruptly fired earlier this year, he was advised by a fellow general now vying to replace him to stop the military’s investigation into an unauthorized helicopter flyby of musician Kid Rock’s Tennessee estate, three people familiar with the matter said. Gen. Randy George, whom Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth removed as the Army chief of staff without explanation, felt it was important to follow typical protocol and determine whether any safety regulations had been violated during the March 28 flyby, these people said. Like some others, they spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss the episode. Gen. Chris LaNeve, the Army’s No. 2 officer, told George that Hegseth did not want the investigation to proceed, one person said. The two others said that George later confided in colleagues about the encounter with LaNeve and seemed troubled by it. George told them that LaNeve suggested it would be best if the review was scuttled, those people said. The revelation, which has not previously been reported, adds a new layer of understanding to Hegseth’s potential motivations for firing George on April 2. Kid Rock, whose legal name is Robert Ritchie, is a vocal supporter of President Donald Trump and avowed critic of many Democratic politicians and causes. Through a spokesman, George, who is now retired, declined to comment. Army officials did not respond to questions about LaNeve, whose candidacy for the chief of staff job faces resistance in Congress. Hegseth, in a statement provided to The Washington Post, did not directly address the discussion between the two generals and described LaNeve as “precisely the kind of leader the U.S. Army needs right now,” interested in strengthening the Army, and “not interested in playing politics in Washington.” “He is a back-to-basics, no politics, no-nonsense General - exactly what President Trump expects,” Hegseth’s statement said. “The critics coming after him are the same out-of-touch so-called insiders who’ve spent years undermining our military with woke policies and endless wars. They hold deep grudges against any commander willing to put America and our troops first, but their days of influence are over.” Sean Parnell, a spokesman for Hegseth, said that the new reporting about George’s departure amounted to a “regurgitating” of a “tired, old story simply to manufacture drama.” Hegseth and his advisers have for months declined to say what precipitated George’s ouster, even when asked directly by Republican and Democratic lawmakers who objected to the firing. He has long been at odds with the service’s senior leadership - including Army Secretary Dan Driscoll, a fellow Trump appointee who at one time was viewed as a potential replacement for Hegseth. Driscoll is now expected to leave the administration soon, perhaps within weeks, officials said. Others familiar with George’s firing have said that multiple factors were probably at play, including his close working relationship with Driscoll. Since taking charge of the Pentagon in January 2025, Hegseth, a former Fox News personality who spent years in the Army National Guard, has overseen the dismissal of more than two dozen top officers. The firings typically occur without cause, though he has complained broadly that the military’s upper ranks are insufficiently loyal to the president or caught in old ways of thinking. Many of those removed have been women and minorities. LaNeve’s actions in the Kid Rock investigation could further complicate his ascension to the Army’s top post. While he has filled the role on an acting basis since George’s ouster nearly five months ago, Trump administration officials have not yet formally nominated him to become the chief of staff amid concerns that he lacks support within the Republican-led Senate Armed Services Committee, said three separate people familiar with the views on Capitol Hill. Sen. Joni Ernst, an Iowa Republican and retired Army National Guard officer initially skeptical of Hegseth’s nomination to lead the Pentagon, opposes LaNeve, these people said. Both George and Gen. James Mingus, another top Army officer forced out by Hegseth, are from Iowa. Without votes from Democrats, nominees require unanimous Republican support on the committee to advance. Ernst’s office did not respond to a request for comment. The Wall Street Journal first reported her opposition to LaNeve. Parnell, Hegseth’s spokesman, downplayed the situation, saying in his statement that Pentagon officials are “actively coordinating with our Senate partners to lock in the optimal moment to formally submit his nomination, and we intend to do so.” On March 31, three days after two AH-64 Apache helicopters flying outside Nashville buzzed the home of Kid Rock, Army officials with the 101st Airborne Division at nearby Fort Campbell announced they were grounding the pilots and launching an administrative investigation. Video shared on social media by the musician showed the aircraft at low altitudes. In his post, he also criticized California Gov. Gavin Newsom, a Democrat who is a frequent critic of the Trump administration. “This is a level of respect,” Kid Rock wrote, that Newsom “will never know.” At the time, the Army said it also was reviewing the flight path of a helicopter that flew the same day over a No Kings protest against Trump in nearby Clarksville, Tennessee. Flight tracker data showed that the aircraft dipped to as low as 625 feet, at one point circling over where protesters were gathered. When the incidents attracted unflattering news coverage, Hegseth promptly intervened. He terminated the Army’s investigation and exonerated the aircrews involved - encouraging them to “Carry on, Patriots.” A few weeks later, Hegseth and Kid Rock flew in Apache helicopters from Fort Belvoir in Virginia, located in suburban D.C. Parnell said then that it was part of a broader community relations event. LaNeve, 59, was not viewed by his Army peers as a likely future chief of staff before the Trump administration came into office, but he caught the president’s attention with a congratulatory call during the Commander-in-Chief Inaugural Ball, people familiar with the matter said. At the time, LaNeve was commanding U.S. soldiers in South Korea and called the president from there. LaNeve was moved into a more influential position as Hegseth’s senior military aide after the defense secretary’s team ousted Lt. Gen. Jennifer Short from the role the following month. This past fall, Hegseth elevated LaNeve again, nominating him to become the Army’s vice chief of staff while forcing Mingus into retirement early. In a May hearing before the House Armed Services Committee, LaNeve faced sharp questions from Republicans over the Pentagon’s decision to cancel the deployment of an Army brigade to Poland, a NATO ally that borders Ukraine. When Rep. Don Bacon (R-Nebraska) asked him about the Poland decision, LaNeve declined to say why the deployment was canceled, arguing he was not part of the military’s “policy side.” “But you’re the chief of staff of the Army,” Bacon responded, noting his acting role. George had been expected to serve as the Army’s chief of staff until fall 2027, completing a typical four-year assignment in the role. Hegseth asked him to retire early during a phone call, news of which was leaked minutes later to CBS News, officials have said previously. The move thwarted any effort by Driscoll, the Army secretary, to save the general’s career before the decision was publicized. Hegseth’s campaign of firings and forced retirements has removed a number of other candidates who may otherwise have been considered for elevation to Army chief of staff, officials said. They include Mingus, who retired early this year; Gen. David Hodne, who was fired without explanation in April; and Gen. Christopher Donahue, who is expected to retire soon after Hegseth stonewalled efforts within the Army and on Capitol Hill to extend his career. Amid the purge, Driscoll has begun to consider his own departure, officials familiar with the matter said. The Wall Street Journal reported Friday that he could leave the Trump administration by the end of the year. That appears likely, officials said, but no firm plan has emerged yet. As The Post and others reported in the immediate aftermath of George’s firing, aides to Hegseth have touted Parnell, the Pentagon spokesman, becoming Army secretary.
